title: Animal Farm
author: George Orwell
tagline: A bundled demo of WhatIfSabha running on Animal Farm.
demo_divergence: What if Boxer killed those dogs when they were trying to chase Snowball away?
synopsis: A group of farm animals revolt against their human master to establish an egalitarian society, only to have their revolution betrayed by the pigs who become as tyrannical as the humans they replaced. The story serves as an allegory for the Russian Revolution and the rise of Stalinism.

timeline.event: The prize boar rallies the animals against human rule. Three nights later he dies.
The animals drive Mr Jones off the farm and raise the green flag.
Snowball and Napoleon share leadership. The Seven Commandments are painted on the barn wall.
Napoleon's dogs chase Snowball off the farm. Napoleon takes sole power.
Boxer works himself to death. The windmill is built and destroyed twice.
The pigs walk on two legs. The final commandment reads: 'All animals are equal, but some are more equal than others.'

knowledge_events.learns: The pigs are sleeping in beds.
knowledge_events.impact_on_character: Causes confusion and erosion of trust in the Commandments.

knowledge_events.learns: The Seven Commandments have been changed.
knowledge_events.impact_on_character: Realization that the revolution has been completely subverted.

character_arcs.name: Napoleon
character_arcs.description: Napoleon is a pig who emerges as the leader of Animal Farm after the rebellion against Mr. Jones. He is cunning, power-hungry, and manipulative, using propaganda and force to consolidate his power. As the story progresses, he becomes increasingly tyrannical and corrupt.

character_arcs.name: Old Major
character_arcs.description: Old Major is a highly respected and wise boar on the farm who has a vision for a better future for all animals. He is the one who inspires the rebellion against Mr. Jones and establishes the principles of Animalism. He is a majestic-looking pig with a benevolent appearance, despite his old age and stoutness.

motivations: to inspire the animals to rebel against Mr. Jones and establish a better future

character_arcs.name: Boxer
character_arcs.description: Boxer is a hardworking and dedicated horse who is deeply committed to the principles of Animalism and the success of the farm. He is known for his strength, loyalty, and unwavering optimism. Despite his physical decline, he remains a symbol of the farm's ideals and a source of inspiration for the other animals.

motivations: to contribute to the success of the farm and the principles of Animalism
to maintain the success of the farm and the principles of Animalism
to continue contributing to the farm, despite growing concerns about the leadership
to survive and hold on to the last vestiges of the farm's ideals

character_arcs.name: Benjamin
character_arcs.description: Benjamin is a wise, aged donkey who has witnessed the rise and fall of the animal rebellion on the farm. He is known for his cynicism and skepticism towards the pigs' leadership. Despite his age, Benjamin remains a steadfast and loyal companion to his fellow animals, particularly Boxer and Clover.

character_arcs.name: Clover
character_arcs.description: Clover is a wise and aged horse who plays a significant role in the story, often serving as a voice of reason and concern. She is a loyal member of the farm community and is particularly close to Benjamin. Clover's character represents a sense of tradition, wisdom, and moral integrity.

character_arcs.name: Mr. Jones
character_arcs.description: Mr. Jones is the owner of the Manor Farm, who is often drunk and neglects his farm, leading to the animals' rebellion. He is a symbol of the old regime and the oppression of the working class. His character serves as a catalyst for the events of the story.

character_arcs.name: Mr. Whymper
character_arcs.description: Mr. Whymper is a solicitor who acts as an intermediary between Animal Farm and the outside world, facilitating trade and communication while being somewhat exploitative and opportunistic.

character_arcs.name: Mr. Pilkington
character_arcs.description: Mr. Pilkington is a neighboring farmer who is initially mentioned as a potential buyer of Animal Farm's produce, but his character evolves to represent the external threat and skepticism towards the farm's success.

motivations: find ways to exploit Animal Farm's situation

character_arcs.name: Snowball
character_arcs.description: advocates for the building of the windmill and is chased away by Napoleon's dogs

character_arcs.name: Squealer
character_arcs.description: explains the new arrangement to the other animals and justifies Napoleon's actions

character_arcs.name: Minimus
character_arcs.description: sits with Napoleon and Squealer on the raised platform and has a gift for composing songs and poems

character_arcs.name: Mr. Frederick
character_arcs.description: is a potential business partner for Napoleon

character_arcs.name: Moses
character_arcs.description: reappears on the farm and tells stories about Sugarcandy Mountain to the other animals

character_arcs.name: Bluebell
character_arcs.description: Bluebell is a horse on Animal Farm, known for her strength and loyalty. She is a hard worker and contributes to the farm's prosperity. Despite her minor role, Bluebell's actions and interactions reveal her character and emotional state throughout the story.

motivations: desire to contribute to the farm's success

character_arcs.name: Jessie
character_arcs.description: Jessie is a minor character in the story Animal Farm, likely one of the animals on the farm, given the context of the story. The specific details about Jessie are not directly provided in the given passages, but based on the story's context, Jessie could be inferred to be involved in the events unfolding on the farm. As a minor character, Jessie's actions and thoughts are not extensively detailed but are part of the collective experience of the animals.

motivations: to be part of something new and revolutionary
to contribute to the farm's success
to avoid conflict and maintain peace
to survive and maintain some level of dignity

character_arcs.name: Muriel
character_arcs.description: Muriel is a goat who lives on Animal Farm, she is a minor character who is not deeply involved in the main events of the story but is part of the community.

motivations: preserving the original ideals of Animalism

character_arcs.name: Mollie
character_arcs.description: Mollie is a self-centered and vain horse who is more concerned with her appearance and social status than with the welfare of the other animals on the farm. She is often depicted as being frivolous and lacking in depth, but also has a certain charm and charisma that makes her a compelling character.

motivations: to maintain her social status and appearance
to contribute to the farm's success and prosperity
to survive and thrive in a changing environment
to escape the farm and find a better life

relationships.description: Napoleon views Snowball as a threat to his absolute authority.
Napoleon exploits Boxer's loyalty and strength for labor.
Squealer acts as the propaganda mouthpiece for Napoleon.
The dogs serve as Napoleon's personal secret police.

divergence_points.description: What if Old Major had lived to lead the revolution himself?
What if Snowball had successfully defended himself against the dogs?
What if the animals had collectively resisted the dogs during the purge?
What if Benjamin had successfully warned Boxer about the van's destination?
What if the animals had allowed Mr. Jones to return after a short period of chaos?
What if the other animals had learned to read and write as well as the pigs?
What if the neighboring farmers had intervened militarily earlier?
What if the windmill had been built successfully without the internal sabotage?

timeline_phases.name: The Rebellion
timeline_phases.description: The animals overthrow Mr. Jones and establish Animalism.
timeline_phases.trigger_event: Old Major's speech and the neglect of the animals by Mr. Jones.

timeline_phases.name: The Golden Age
timeline_phases.description: Initial success and unity under the Seven Commandments.
timeline_phases.trigger_event: The successful harvest and the Battle of the Cowshed.

timeline_phases.name: The Rise of Dictatorship
timeline_phases.description: Napoleon consolidates power through force and propaganda.
timeline_phases.trigger_event: The expulsion of Snowball by the dogs.

timeline_phases.name: The Totalitarian State
timeline_phases.description: The pigs fully adopt human vices and oppress the other animals.
timeline_phases.trigger_event: The final transformation of the Seven Commandments.

key_events.name: Old Major's Speech
key_events.description: Old Major inspires the animals to dream of a world without human tyranny.
key_events.consequence: The seeds of the Rebellion are planted.

key_events.name: Expulsion of Snowball
key_events.description: Napoleon uses his trained dogs to chase Snowball off the farm.
key_events.consequence: Napoleon gains absolute control over the farm.

key_events.name: The Great Purge
key_events.description: Napoleon executes animals who 'confess' to conspiring with Snowball.
key_events.consequence: Fear becomes the primary tool of governance.

key_events.name: Death of Boxer
key_events.description: Napoleon sells the loyal, dying Boxer to a glue boiler.
key_events.consequence: The final moral collapse of the farm's leadership.

qa.question: Why pick Animal Farm for the demo?
qa.answer: It is short, tightly plotted, public domain in most jurisdictions, and every major character has a clear stake in the revolution — or a clear reason to betray it. That makes it ideal for counterfactuals: change one thing early and the whole arc bends in a way you can argue about.

qa.question: Is the demo using the real book text?
qa.answer: No. The app uploads a PDF, extracts the cast and their personalities, and the characters then speak from those extracted profiles. Nothing any character says in the debate is a quote from Orwell — every line is generated by an AI playing that character.

qa.question: Who actually wins at the end of the book?
qa.answer: Nobody the reader is asked to root for. The pigs win power, the humans keep their farms, and the working animals lose everything they fought for. Orwell leaves the farm permanently worse off than it started — which is precisely why the 'what if' questions hit so hard.
